Craving should be contemplated as suffering; craving should be contemplated as non-self; craving should be contemplated as peace.
Craving should be reflected upon as secluded;
craving should be reflected upon as a disease; craving should be reflected upon as an abscess.
Craving should be contemplated as a thorn; craving should be contemplated as a slaughter; craving should be contemplated as an affliction.
Craving should be reflected upon as being dependent on others;
craving should be reflected upon as having the nature of disintegration; craving should be reflected upon as being unstable.
Craving should be contemplated as fragile,
craving should be contemplated as fearful,
and craving should be contemplated as a calamity.
Craving should be contemplated as empty; craving should be contemplated as not belonging to a self;
craving should be contemplated as unreliable.
Craving should be attended to as an affliction,
and that by way of non-apprehension,
through the production of the thought associated with the knowledge of all aspects.
Grasping should be contemplated as impermanent;
grasping should be contemplated as suffering;
grasping should be contemplated as non-self.
Grasping should be attended to as peaceful; grasping should be attended to as secluded;
grasping should be attended to as a disease.
Grasping should be attended to as a tumor; grasping should be attended to as a thorn;
grasping should be attended to as a calamity.
Grasping should be contemplated as a disease;
grasping should be contemplated as alien;
grasping should be contemplated as subject to disintegration.
Grasping should be contemplated as unstable; grasping should be contemplated as fragile;
grasping should be contemplated as fearful.
Grasping should be contemplated as a defilement;
grasping should be contemplated as empty;
grasping should be contemplated as not-self.
Grasping should be attended to as unreliable, grasping should be attended to as afflictive,
and that by way of non-apprehension.
With a thought associated with the knowledge of all aspects,
existence should be reflected upon as impermanent;
existence should be reflected upon as suffering.
Existence should be contemplated as selfless; existence should be contemplated as peaceful;
existence should be contemplated as secluded.
Existence should be contemplated as a disease; existence should be contemplated as an abscess; existence should be contemplated as a thorn.
Existence should be reflected upon as a calamity; existence should be reflected upon as a disease;
existence should be reflected upon as the enemy.
Existence should be contemplated as subject to destruction; existence should be contemplated as unstable;
existence should be contemplated as fragile.
Existence should be contemplated as fear; existence should be contemplated as a calamity;
existence should be contemplated as empty.
Existence should be contemplated as not belonging to a self;
existence should be contemplated as unreliable;
existence should be contemplated as afflictive.
And that should be done by way of non-apprehension.
With a thought associated with the knowledge of all aspects,
birth should be reflected upon as impermanent.
Birth should be contemplated as suffering; birth should be contemplated as non-self;
birth should be contemplated as peace.
Birth should be reflected upon as solitude; birth should be reflected upon as a disease;
birth should be reflected upon as a tumor.
Birth should be reflected upon as a thorn; birth should be reflected upon as a calamity; birth should be reflected upon as an affliction.
Birth should be reflected upon as something dependent on others;
birth should be reflected upon as subject to the nature of dissolution; birth should be reflected upon as unstable.
Birth should be reflected upon as fragile, birth should be reflected upon as fearful,
and birth should be reflected upon as a calamity.
Birth should be contemplated as empty; birth should be contemplated as not-self;
birth should be contemplated as unreliable.
Birth should be reflected upon in terms of its afflictive nature,
and that by way of non-apprehension,
through the production of the thought of awakening associated with the knowledge of all aspects.
Old age and death should be contemplated as impermanent;
old age and death should be contemplated as suffering;
old age and death should be contemplated as non-self.
Old age and death should be contemplated as peaceful;
old age and death should be contemplated as secluded;
old age and death should be contemplated as a disease.
Old age and death should be attended to as a boil; old age and death should be attended to as a thorn;
old age and death should be attended to as a calamity.
Old age and death should be attended to as an affliction;
old age and death should be attended to as external;
old age and death should be attended to as subject to disintegration.
Old age and death should be reflected upon as being unstable; old age and death should be reflected upon as being fragile;
old age and death should be reflected upon as being fearful.
Old age and death should be reflected upon as an affliction;
old age and death should be reflected upon as empty;
old age and death should be reflected upon as not belonging to a self.
Old age and death should be reflected upon as being unreliable;
old age and death should be reflected upon as being afflictive,
and that by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, by way of non-apprehension; he practices the perfection of ethical discipline with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, by way of non-apprehension;
he practices the perfection of patience with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, by way of non-apprehension.
With mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he practices the perfection of vigor by way of non-apprehension;

with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he practices the perfection of meditation by way of non-apprehension; and with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he practices the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness with thoughts associated with the knowledge of all aspects, by way of non-apprehension;
he cultivates the four right efforts with thoughts associated with the knowledge of all aspects, by way of non-apprehension;
he cultivates the four bases of psychic power with thoughts associated with the knowledge of all aspects, by way of non-apprehension.

By means of mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, one cultivates the five faculties through the yoga of non-apprehension; by means of mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, one cultivates the five powers through the yoga of non-apprehension;
by means of mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment through the yoga of non-apprehension.

With mind-sets associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the eightfold noble path by way of non-apprehension; with mind-sets associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the four noble truths by way of non-apprehension;
with mind-sets associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the four meditative concentrations by way of non-apprehension.
By means of mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, one cultivates the four immeasurables through the yoga of non-apprehension;
by means of mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, one cultivates the four formless attainments through the yoga of non-apprehension.
With mind-orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the eight liberations by way of non-apprehension;
with mind-orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the serial attainments of meditative dwelling by way of non-apprehension;
and with mind-orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—by way of non-apprehension.

With mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, one cultivates the superknowledges through the yoga of non-apprehension; with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, one cultivates the meditative concentrations through the yoga of non-apprehension;
and with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, one cultivates the gateways of mnemonic formulas through the yoga of non-apprehension.
With mind-sets associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the ten powers of a Tathāgata through the yoga of non-apprehension;
with mind-sets associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the four grounds of self-confidence through the yoga of non-apprehension;
with mind-sets associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates the four analytical knowledges through the yoga of non-apprehension.
They cultivate great loving-kindness through the yoga of non-apprehension by means of thought-moments associated with the knowledge of all aspects;

they cultivate great compassion through the yoga of non-apprehension by means of thought-moments associated with the knowledge of all aspects; and they cultivate the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha through the yoga of non-apprehension by means of thought-moments associated with the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom trains himself thus:
"These very phenomena moisten, drench, fulfill, pervade, and investigate other phenomena;
herein there is no self or anything belonging to a self. Why is that?"
For instance, that mind of dedication belonging to a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not contained within the mind of awakening,
and that mind of awakening is not contained within the mind of dedication;
O Kauśika, that mind of dedication does not exist and is not apprehended within the mind of awakening.

That which is the thought of awakening does not exist and is not apprehended within the thought of dedication. This, Kauśika, is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in that he thus examines all phenomena and yet does not course in any phenomena whatsoever.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the elder Subhūti as follows:
Venerable Subhūti, how is it that the mind of dedication is not contained within the mind of awakening? How is it that the mind of awakening is not contained within the mind of dedication?
How is it that the mind of dedication does not exist and is not apprehended within the mind of awakening?
(ŚsP II-2 138) How is it that the thought of awakening does not exist and is not apprehended within the thought of dedication?
Subhūti said:
Kauśika, that mind of dedication is no-mind;
that mind of awakening is no-mind.
For that which is no-mind is inconceivable.
That which is inconceivable is mindless; for mindlessness does not dedicate itself to mindlessness, nor does inconceivability dedicate itself to inconceivability.
For indeed, that which is mindlessness is inconceivability, and that which is inconceivability is mindlessness.
"This, Kauśika, is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is indeed excellent that you instruct the bodhisattva mahāsattvas in the perfection of wisdom and inspire them with enthusiasm."
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, I must be grateful and not ungrateful;
for it was by those disciples in the presence of the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas that [this Dharma] was [attained]."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, while formerly a bodhisattva, was exhorted, instructed, demonstrated, encouraged, inspired, established, and settled in the six perfections;
since, O Blessed One, while formerly a bodhisattva, he trained in the six perfections, [he attained] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"O Blessed One, it is exactly so; we must instruct, train, gladden, and encourage the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, in the six perfections."
They should be led across, gladdened, settled, and established.

"We too have instructed, exhorted, gladdened, incited, inspired, delighted, established, and settled the bodhisattva mahāsattvas in the six perfections; they shall fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

Therefore, Kauśika, listen well and attend closely; I shall speak. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom in such a way, and should not abide in such a way: Kauśika, form is empty of form;
feeling is empty of feeling.
Perception is empty of perception; mental formations are empty of mental formations;
consciousness is empty of consciousness.
“A bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva.

For in this way, Kauśika, the emptiness of form, the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of perception, the emptiness of mental formations, the emptiness of consciousness, and the emptiness of a bodhisattva—these are non-dual and not divided into two. It is thus indeed, Kauśika.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the eye is empty of the eye, and the ear is empty of the ear.
The nose is empty; the nose is empty of the nose.
The tongue is empty; the tongue is empty of the tongue.
The body is empty; the body is empty of the body.
The mind is empty of mind;
the bodhisattva is empty of bodhisattva.
For thus, Kauśika, there is the emptiness of the eye, the emptiness of the ear, the emptiness of the nose, and the emptiness of the tongue.

The emptiness of the body, the emptiness of the mind, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva—these are non-dual and not divided into two. In this way, indeed, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Kauśika, form is empty of form.
Sound is empty of sound; odor is empty of odor;
taste is empty of taste.
Contact is empty of contact; phenomena are empty of phenomena;
the bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva.
Thus, Kauśika, the emptiness of form, the emptiness of sound, the emptiness of odor, the emptiness of taste, the emptiness of tangibles,
the emptiness of phenomena, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva— these are non-dual and not divided into two. In this way, Kauśika,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, eye-consciousness is empty of eye-consciousness;
ear-consciousness is empty of ear-consciousness;
nose-consciousness is empty of nose-consciousness.
Tongue-consciousness is empty of tongue-consciousness;
body-consciousness is empty of body-consciousness;
mind-consciousness is empty of mind-consciousness.
A bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva;

for in this way, Kauśika, the emptiness of eye-consciousness, the emptiness of ear-consciousness, the emptiness of nose-consciousness, the emptiness of tongue-consciousness, the emptiness of body-consciousness, and the emptiness of mind-consciousness are the same as the emptiness of a bodhisattva.
And this is non-dual, without division. In this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Kauśika, eye-contact is empty of eye-contact;
ear-contact is empty of ear-contact.
Olfactory contact is empty of olfactory contact; gustatory contact is empty of gustatory contact;
tactile contact is empty of tactile contact.
Mental contact is empty of mental contact;
a bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva.
For thus, Kauśika, there is the emptiness of eye-contact, the emptiness of ear-contact, and the emptiness of nose-contact.

And the emptiness of tongue-contact, the emptiness of body-contact, and the emptiness of mind-contact, as well as the emptiness of the bodhisattva—these are non-dual and not divided into two. In this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, feeling born of eye-contact is empty of feeling born of eye-contact.
Feeling born of ear-contact is empty of feeling born of ear-contact; feeling born of nose-contact is empty of feeling born of nose-contact;
feeling born of tongue-contact is [empty of feeling born of tongue-contact].
Feeling born of tongue-contact is empty of feeling born of tongue-contact; feeling born of body-contact is empty of feeling born of body-contact;
feeling born of mind-contact is empty of feeling born of mind-contact.
A bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva; for thus, Kauśika, the emptiness of feeling born of eye-contact, the emptiness of feeling born of ear-contact,
the emptiness of feeling born of nose-contact, the emptiness of feeling born of tongue-contact, and the emptiness of feeling born of body-contact [are likewise].
And the emptiness of feeling born of mind-contact and the emptiness of the bodhisattva—these are non-dual and not divided into two.
Thus, Kausika, a bodhisattva mahasattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kausika, the earth element is empty of the earth element.
The water element is empty of the water element;
the fire element is empty of the fire element;
the air element is empty of the air element.
The space element is empty of the space element;
the consciousness element is empty of the consciousness element;
the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
For thus, Kauśika, the emptiness of the earth element, the emptiness of the water element, the emptiness of the fire element, the emptiness of the wind element,

the emptiness of the space element, the emptiness of the consciousness element, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva— these are non-dual and not divided into two. It is in this way, Kauśika, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, ignorance is empty of ignorance;
volitional formations are empty of volitional formations;
consciousness is empty of consciousness.
Name-and-form is empty of name-and-form; the six sense bases are empty of the six sense bases;
contact is empty of contact.
Feeling is empty of feeling; craving is empty of craving;
grasping is empty of grasping.
Existence is empty of existence; birth is empty of birth;
old age and death are empty of old age and death.
A bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva;
for thus, Kauśika, the emptiness of ignorance, the emptiness of formative volitions, the emptiness of consciousness, the emptiness of name-and-form,
the emptiness of the six sense bases, the emptiness of contact, the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of craving, and the emptiness of grasping [are all likewise].

The emptiness of existence, the emptiness of birth, the emptiness of old age and death, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva—these are non-dual and not divided into two. In this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the perfection of giving is empty of the perfection of giving.
The perfection of ethical discipline is empty of the perfection of ethical discipline;
the perfection of patience is empty of the perfection of patience;
the perfection of vigor is empty of the perfection of vigor.
The perfection of meditation is empty of the perfection of meditation;
the perfection of wisdom is empty of the perfection of wisdom;
the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

For thus, Kauśika, the emptiness of the perfection of giving and the emptiness of the perfection of morality, the emptiness of the perfection of patience and the emptiness of the perfection of vigor, the emptiness of the perfection of meditation and the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva—
these are non-dual and not divided into two.
In this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, internal emptiness is empty of internal emptiness;
external emptiness is empty of external emptiness.
Internal-external emptiness is empty of internal-external emptiness;
the emptiness of emptiness is empty of the emptiness of emptiness;
great emptiness is empty of great emptiness.
Ultimate emptiness is empty of ultimate emptiness;
conditioned emptiness is empty of conditioned emptiness;
unconditioned emptiness is empty of unconditioned emptiness.
Absolute emptiness is empty of absolute emptiness;
emptiness without beginning or end is empty of emptiness without beginning or end;
emptiness of non-dispersal is empty of emptiness of non-dispersal.
The emptiness of intrinsic nature is empty of the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
the emptiness of all phenomena is empty of the emptiness of all phenomena;
the emptiness of specific characteristics is empty of the emptiness of specific characteristics.
Non-apprehension emptiness is empty of non-apprehension emptiness;
non-existence emptiness is empty of non-existence emptiness;
self-nature emptiness is empty of self-nature emptiness.
The emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is empty by virtue of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
a bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva.
Thus, Kauśika, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, and the emptiness of emptiness [are all empty].

and great emptiness, and ultimate emptiness, and conditioned emptiness, and unconditioned emptiness, and absolute emptiness, and emptiness without beginning or end, and emptiness of non-dispersal, and natural emptiness, and emptiness of all phenomena, and emptiness of specific characteristics,
and emptiness of non-apprehension, and emptiness of non-existence, and emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the non-existent intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva.
And this is non-dual and indivisible. In this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the foundations of mindfulness are empty of the foundations of mindfulness;
the right efforts are empty of the right efforts.
The bases of psychic power are empty of the bases of psychic power; the faculties are empty of the faculties;
the powers are empty of the powers.
The factors of enlightenment are empty of the factors of enlightenment;
the noble eightfold path is empty of the noble eightfold path;
the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

Thus, Kauśika, the emptiness of the applications of mindfulness, the emptiness of the right efforts, the emptiness of the bases of psychic power, the emptiness of the faculties, the emptiness of the powers, the emptiness of the factors of enlightenment, the emptiness of the path, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva—
these are non-dual and not divided into two. It is in this way, Kauśika, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the noble truths are empty of the noble truths;
the meditative concentrations are empty of the meditative concentrations;
the immeasurables are empty of the immeasurables.
The formless attainments are empty of formless attainments;
the liberations are empty of liberations.
The successive attainments of meditative dwelling are empty of the successive attainments of meditative dwelling;
the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are empty of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the supernormal powers are empty of the supernormal powers.
The concentrations are empty of concentrations; the doors of dhāraṇī are empty of the doors of dhāraṇī;
the powers of a Tathāgata are empty of the powers of a Tathāgata.
The grounds of self-confidence are empty of the grounds of self-confidence;
the analytical knowledges are empty of the analytical knowledges;
great loving-kindness is empty of great loving-kindness.
Great compassion is empty of great compassion;
the unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of the unique qualities of a Buddha;
a bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva.

For in this way, Kauśika, the emptiness of the noble truths and the emptiness of the meditative concentrations, the emptiness of the immeasurables, the emptiness of the formless attainments, the emptiness of the liberations,

the emptiness of the successive dwellings and attainments, the emptiness of the gateways to liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— the emptiness of the superknowledges, the emptiness of the meditative absorptions, the emptiness of the gateways to the dhāraṇīs, and the emptiness of the powers of a Tathāgata.
The emptiness of the fearlessnesses, the emptiness of the analytical knowledges, the emptiness of great loving-kindness, the emptiness of great compassion,

the emptiness of the unique qualities of a buddha, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva— these are non-dual and not divided into two. It is in this way, Kauśika, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the vehicle of the śrāvakas is empty of the vehicle of the śrāvakas;
the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas is empty of the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas; the vehicle of the buddhas is empty of the vehicle of the buddhas;
and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

For thus, the emptiness of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the emptiness of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the emptiness of the Buddha vehicle, and the emptiness of the Bodhisattva are non-dual and not divided into two. In this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Kauśika, a śrāvaka is empty of being a śrāvaka.
A pratyekabuddha is empty of a pratyekabuddha; a buddha is empty of a buddha;
a bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva.

Thus, indeed, the emptiness of the śrāvaka, the emptiness of the pratyekabuddha, the emptiness of the Buddha, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva—these are non-dual and not divided into two. In this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the fruit of stream-entry is empty of the fruit of stream-entry.
The fruit of once-returning is empty of the fruit of once-returning;
the fruit of non-returning is empty of the fruit of non-returning;
arhatship is empty of arhatship.
Pratyekabodhi is empty of pratyekabodhi;
the knowledge of the aspects of the path is empty of the knowledge of the aspects of the path;
and the knowledge of all aspects is empty of the knowledge of all aspects.

A bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva; for indeed, the emptiness of the fruit of stream-entry, the emptiness of the fruit of once-returning, the emptiness of the fruit of non-returning, the emptiness of the fruit of arhatship, the emptiness of solitary awakening, and the emptiness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path [are likewise empty].

And the emptiness of the knowledge of all modes and the emptiness of the bodhisattva—these are non-dual; they are not divided into two. It is indeed in this way, Kauśika, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should [not] abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the elder Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not abide in the perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti said:
"Thus, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should not abide in form by way of apprehension,
nor should he abide in feeling by way of apprehension."
One should not abide in perception by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in mental formations by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in consciousness by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in the eye by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the ear by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the nose by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in the tongue by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the body by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the mind by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in form by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in sound by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in odor by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in taste by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in touch by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in mental phenomena by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in eye-consciousness by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in ear-consciousness by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in nose-consciousness by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in tongue-consciousness by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in body-consciousness by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in mind-consciousness by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in eye-contact by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in ear-contact by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in nose-contact by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in tongue-contact by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in body-contact by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in mind-contact by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in feeling born of eye-contact by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in feeling born of ear-contact by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in feeling born of nose-contact by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in feeling born of tongue-contact by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in feeling born of body-contact by way of apprehension; [one should not abide] in feeling born of mind-contact.
One should not abide in feeling by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in the earth element by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the water element by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in the fire element by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the wind element by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the space element by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in the element of consciousness by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in ignorance by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in formative forces by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in consciousness by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in name-and-form by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the six sense bases by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in contact by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in feeling by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in craving by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in grasping by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in becoming by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in birth by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in old age and death by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the perfection of generosity by way of apprehension,
nor should one abide in the perfection of ethical discipline by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in the perfection of patience by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the perfection of vigor by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the perfection of meditation by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in the perfection of wisdom by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in internal emptiness by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in external emptiness by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in internal-external emptiness by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in the emptiness of emptiness by way of apprehension;
one should not abide in great emptiness by way of apprehension.
One should not abide in the emptiness of the ultimate through the application of apprehension;
one should not abide in the emptiness of the conditioned through the application of apprehension;
one should not abide in the emptiness of the unconditioned through the application of apprehension.
One should not abide in absolute emptiness by way of apprehension; one should not abide in the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end by way of apprehension;

One should not abide by way of apprehension [thinking]: "there would be no term for the emptiness of non-existence, there would be no term for the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and there would be no term for the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence";

nor should one abide by way of apprehension [thinking]: "there would be no term for the applications of mindfulness, there would be no term for the right efforts, and there would be no term for the bases of psychic power."

One should not abide in the notion that there would be no term for the faculties, no term for the powers, no term for the factors of enlightenment, no term for the noble eightfold path, and no term for the noble truths—by way of apprehension;

nor should one abide in the notion that there would be no term for the meditative concentrations, no term for the immeasurables, no term for the formless attainments, and no term for the liberations—by way of apprehension;
nor should one abide in the notion that there would be no term for the serial attainments, nor no term for the gateways to liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

One should not abide by way of apprehension with the thought, "May there be no word for the superknowledges, may there be no word for meditative concentration, may there be no word for the gateways of mnemonic formulas";

nor should one abide by way of apprehension with the thought, "May there be no word for the powers of a Tathāgata, may there be no word for the grounds of self-confidence, may there be no word for the analytical knowledges."
One should not abide in the thought, by way of apprehension, that "there would be no sound of great loving-kindness, no sound of great compassion, and no sound of the unique qualities of a Buddha";
nor should one abide in the thought, by way of apprehension, that "there would be no sound of stream-entry, no sound of once-returning, no sound of non-returning, and no sound of arhatship";
nor should one abide in the thought, by way of apprehension, that "there would be no sound of a pratyekabuddha and no sound of a Buddha. Why is that?
For thus, by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, no phenomena were apprehended.
In this way indeed, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the perfection of wisdom by means of apprehension.
Then, this thought occurred to the Venerable Śāradvatīputra:
Furthermore, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the perfection of wisdom?

Then, the venerable Subhūti, knowing the reflection in the mind of the venerable Śāradvatīputra by means of his own mind, addressed the venerable Śāradvatīputra: "What do you think, venerable Śāradvatīputra, where does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha, abide?"

He said: "Venerable Subhūti, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, does not abide anywhere; indeed, Venerable Subhūti, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, has a mind that is non-abiding. He does not abide in form, he does not abide in feeling, he does not abide in perception, he does not abide in mental formations, and he does not abide in consciousness."
He does not abide in the eye, nor does he abide in the ear, nor does he abide in the nose, nor does he abide in the tongue, nor does he abide in the body, nor does he abide in the mind.
He does not abide in forms, nor does he abide in sounds, nor does he abide in odors, nor does he abide in tastes, nor does he abide in tangibles, nor does he abide in mental phenomena.

He does not abide in eye-consciousness, he does not abide in ear-consciousness, he does not abide in nose-consciousness, he does not abide in tongue-consciousness, he does not abide in body-consciousness, and he does not abide in mind-consciousness.

He does not abide in eye-contact, he does not abide in ear-contact, he does not abide in nose-contact, he does not abide in tongue-contact, he does not abide in body-contact, and he does not abide in mind-contact.
He does not abide in the feeling conditioned by eye-contact, nor does he abide in the feeling conditioned by ear-contact.

He does not abide in sensation conditioned by olfactory contact; he does not abide in sensation conditioned by gustatory contact; he does not abide in sensation conditioned by tactile contact; he does not abide in sensation conditioned by mental contact.

He does not abide in the earth element; he does not abide in the water element; he does not abide in the fire element; he does not abide in the wind element; he does not abide in the space element; he does not abide in the consciousness element.

He does not abide in ignorance, nor does he abide in volitional formations, nor does he abide in consciousness, nor does he abide in name-and-form, nor does he abide in the six sense bases, nor does he abide in contact, nor does he abide in feeling, nor does he abide in craving, nor does he abide in grasping, nor does he abide in existence, nor does he abide in birth, nor does he abide in old age and death.

He does not abide in the perfection of generosity, nor does he abide in the perfection of ethical discipline, nor does he abide in the perfection of patience, nor does he abide in the perfection of vigor, nor does he abide in the perfection of meditative concentration, nor does he abide in the perfection of wisdom;

he does not abide in internal emptiness, nor does he abide in external emptiness, nor does he abide in internal and external emptiness, nor does he abide in the emptiness of emptiness, nor does he abide in great emptiness, nor does he abide in the emptiness of the ultimate.

He does not abide in the emptiness of the conditioned, he does not abide in the emptiness of the unconditioned, he does not abide in absolute emptiness, he does not abide in the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, he does not abide in the emptiness of non-dispersal, he does not abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
he does not abide in the emptiness of all phenomena, he does not abide in the emptiness of specific characteristics, nor does he abide in the emptiness of non-apprehension.
He does not abide in the emptiness of non-existence; he does not abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature; he does not abide in the emptiness of both non-existence and intrinsic nature.

He does not abide in the applications of mindfulness; he does not abide in the right efforts; he does not abide in the bases of psychic power; he does not abide in the faculties; he does not abide in the powers; he does not abide in the factors of enlightenment; he does not abide in the noble eightfold path; nor does he abide in the noble truths.

He does not abide in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), he does not abide in the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), he does not abide in the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), he does not abide in the liberations (*vimokṣa*), he does not abide in the serial attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), he does not abide in the gateways to liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (*śūnyatānimittāpraṇihitavimokṣamukha*),
he does not abide in the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), he does not abide in the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), and he does not abide in the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*).

He does not abide in the powers of a Tathāgata; he does not abide in the grounds of self-confidence; he does not abide in the analytical knowledges; he does not abide in great loving-kindness; he does not abide in great compassion; he does not abide in the unique qualities of a Buddha; he does not abide in omniscience;
he does not abide in the knowledge of the aspects of the path; he does not abide in the knowledge of all aspects.
Subhūti said: "In this way indeed, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should stand in the perfection of wisdom—
just as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha neither stands nor does not stand in form, nor in feeling."
He is neither established nor unestablished in perception; he is neither established nor unestablished in mental formations; he is neither established nor unestablished in consciousness.

He is neither established nor unestablished in the eye; he is neither established nor unestablished in the ear; he is neither established nor unestablished in the nose; he is neither established nor unestablished in the tongue; he is neither established nor unestablished in the body.
He is neither non-abiding in the mind, nor abiding, nor non-abiding.

He is neither abiding in form, nor non-abiding; he is neither abiding in sound, nor non-abiding; he is neither abiding in odor, nor non-abiding; he is neither abiding in taste, nor non-abiding; he is neither abiding in tangibles, nor non-abiding;
he is neither abiding in mental phenomena, nor non-abiding.

He is neither established nor not established in eye-consciousness; he is neither established nor not established in ear-consciousness; he is neither established nor not established in nose-consciousness; he is neither established nor not established in tongue-consciousness; he is neither established nor not established in body-consciousness; he is neither established nor not established in mind-consciousness.

He is neither stationed nor not stationed in visual contact; he is neither stationed nor not stationed in auditory contact; he is neither stationed nor not stationed in olfactory contact; he is neither stationed nor not stationed in gustatory contact; he is neither stationed nor not stationed in tactile contact; he is neither stationed nor not stationed in mental contact.
He neither stands nor does not stand in the feeling conditioned by eye-contact; he neither stands nor does not stand in the feeling conditioned by ear-contact;

he neither stands nor does not stand in the feeling conditioned by nose-contact; he neither stands nor does not stand in the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact; he neither stands nor does not stand in the feeling conditioned by body-contact; [he neither stands nor does not stand] in the feeling conditioned by mind-contact.

It is neither situated nor not situated in the earth element; it is neither situated nor not situated in the water element; it is neither situated nor not situated in the fire element; it is neither situated nor not situated in the wind element; it is neither situated nor not situated in the space element.
He does not abide in the element of consciousness, nor does he not abide;

he does not abide in ignorance, nor does he not abide; he does not abide in formative forces, nor does he not abide; he does not abide in consciousness, nor does he not abide; he does not abide in name-and-form, nor does he not abide; he does not abide in the six sense bases, nor does he not abide; [he does not abide] in contact...
He is neither established nor unestablished in feeling;

he is neither established nor unestablished in craving; he is neither established nor unestablished in grasping; he is neither established nor unestablished in becoming; he is neither established nor unestablished in birth; he is neither established nor unestablished in aging and death. He is neither established nor unestablished.

He neither stands nor does not stand in the perfection of generosity; he neither stands nor does not stand in the perfection of ethical discipline; he neither stands nor does not stand in the perfection of patience; he neither stands nor does not stand in the perfection of vigor; he neither stands nor does not stand in the perfection of meditative concentration; he neither stands nor does not stand in the perfection of wisdom.
He is neither established nor unestablished in internal emptiness; he is neither established nor unestablished in external emptiness;
he is neither established nor unestablished in internal-and-external emptiness; he is neither established nor unestablished in the emptiness of emptiness;
he is neither established nor unestablished in great emptiness; he is neither established nor unestablished in the emptiness of the ultimate.
He is neither established nor unestablished in the emptiness of the conditioned; he is neither established nor unestablished in the emptiness of the unconditioned;
he is neither established nor unestablished in absolute emptiness; he is neither established nor unestablished in the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end;
he is neither established nor unestablished in the emptiness of non-dispersal; he is neither established nor unestablished in the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
He is neither abiding nor non-abiding in the emptiness of all phenomena; he is neither abiding nor non-abiding in the emptiness of specific characteristics;
he is neither abiding nor non-abiding in the emptiness of the non-apprehendable; he is neither abiding nor non-abiding in the emptiness of non-existence;
he is neither abiding nor non-abiding in the emptiness of intrinsic nature; and he is neither abiding nor non-abiding in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
Neither abiding nor non-abiding:
he neither abides nor does not abide in the applications of mindfulness;
he neither abides nor does not abide in the right efforts.
He neither stands nor does not stand upon the bases of psychic power; he neither stands nor does not stand upon the faculties;
he neither stands nor does not stand upon the powers.
He is neither established nor unestablished in the factors of enlightenment; he is neither established nor unestablished in the noble eightfold path;
he is neither established nor unestablished in the noble truths.
He is neither established nor unestablished in the meditative absorptions;
he is neither established nor unestablished in the immeasurables;
he is neither established nor unestablished in the formless attainments.
He is neither established nor not established in the liberations; he is neither established nor not established in the successive meditative attainments;
he is neither established nor not established in the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He is neither established nor unestablished in the superknowledges;
he is neither established nor unestablished in the meditative concentrations;
he is neither established nor unestablished in the gateways of the dhāraṇīs.

He is neither established nor unestablished in the powers of a Tathāgata; he is neither established nor unestablished in the grounds of self-confidence; he is neither established nor unestablished in the analytical knowledges.
He neither abides nor does not abide in great loving-kindness;
he neither abides nor does not abide in great compassion;
he neither abides nor does not abide in the unique qualities of a Buddha.
He is neither established nor unestablished in omniscience; he is neither established nor unestablished in the knowledge of the aspects of the path;
he is neither established nor unestablished in the knowledge of all aspects.
"In this way indeed, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in and abide in the perfection of wisdom by means of the yoga of non-abiding.
Then, in that assembly, this thought occurred to some of the sons of the gods:
Those yakṣa-words, yakṣa-mantras, yakṣa-sounds, and yakṣa-utterances that are understood when they are being recited— these are indeed understood;
yet this which the noble Subhūti speaks, utters, teaches, analyzes, clarifies, and instructs regarding the perfection of wisdom is not understood.
Then the Venerable Subhūti, having known with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those sons of the gods, addressed those sons of the gods:
"Sons of the gods, it is not understood what you are saying.
The sons of the gods said:
"It is not cognized, O Noble Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"For indeed, O sons of gods, not even a single syllable has been uttered; that which is not uttered is not heard, and that which is not heard is not cognized. For what reason?"
For syllables are not the perfection of wisdom, nor is there here anyone who teaches, anyone who hears, or anyone who understands. Why is that?

Because, O sons of gods, the awakening of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones is indeed beyond syllables. It is just as if, O sons of gods, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One were to create a magical emanation of a Buddha. And that [emanation], in turn...

An emanation might manifest four assemblies—an emanation of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—and then that emanation might teach the Dharma to those four manifested assemblies. What do you think, sons of the gods? Would anything have been taught there in that assembly by anyone at all?
"Could it have been heard or understood by anyone?
They replied, "Certainly not, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
In the same way, sons of gods, all phenomena are like magical emanations; therein, nothing has been taught by anyone, nothing has been heard by anyone, and nothing has been understood by anyone.

It is just as if, sons of gods, a man who has entered a dream were to see a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, teaching the Dharma. What do you think, sons of gods? Would anything therein have been taught, or heard, or understood?
They said: "Certainly not, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"In just this way, sons of gods, all phenomena are like a dream; therein nothing has been taught by anyone, nor has anything been heard by anyone."

"O sons of the gods, it has not been heard nor understood by anyone that, for example, two men standing in a mountain cave might speak the praises of the Buddha, speak the praises of the Dharma, and speak the praises of the Saṅgha, and from both sides an echo of their voice would emerge. What do you think?"
"O sons of gods, would that second echo-sound be made known by that single echo-sound?
They replied, "Certainly not, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
In the same way, O sons of the gods, all phenomena are like an echo;
therein, nothing has been taught by anyone, nothing has been heard by anyone, and nothing has been understood by anyone.
It is just as if, O sons of the gods, a skilled illusionist or an apprentice of an illusionist were to manifest a Tathāgata at a crossroads of four great roads.

He emanates an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, and he emanates the four assemblies— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen— and that emanation might teach the Dharma to those emanated assemblies. What do you think, sons of the gods?
"Could it be that anyone there has taught it, heard it, or understood it?
They replied, "Certainly not, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
In the same way, O sons of gods, all phenomena are like an illusion; therein nothing has been heard by anyone, nothing has been taught by anyone, and nothing has been understood by anyone.
Then this thought occurred to those sons of gods:
"Ah, this noble elder Subhūti will further clarify [this matter]; ah, this noble elder Subhūti will make the perfection of wisdom clear!"
And yet, he teaches what is even more profound than the profound;
he enters into what is even more subtle than the subtle.
Then the venerable Subhūti, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those sons of the gods, addressed those sons of the gods as follows:
Indeed, O sons of gods, form is neither profound nor subtle;
sensation is neither profound nor subtle;
perception is neither profound nor subtle.
Formations are neither deep nor subtle;
consciousness is neither deep nor subtle. Why is that?
Because the intrinsic nature of form is neither deep nor subtle.

Then, this thought occurred to those sons of the gods:
"Indeed, in this teaching of the Dharma, no form has been designated."

Feeling conditioned by eye-contact has not been designated.
Feeling conditioned by ear-contact has not been designated; feeling conditioned by nose-contact has not been designated;
feeling conditioned by tongue-contact has not been designated.
Neither feeling conditioned by body-contact has been designated, nor feeling conditioned by mind-contact has been designated.
Neither the earth element has been designated, nor...
The water element is not designated,
the fire element is not designated,
and the wind element is not designated.
The element of space has not been designated,
nor has the element of consciousness been designated. Ignorance has not been designated.
Formations have not been designated; consciousness has not been designated; name-and-form has not been designated.
The six sense bases have not been designated, contact has not been designated, and feeling has not been designated.
Craving has not been designated,
grasping has not been designated,
and becoming has not been designated.
Birth was not designated, nor was aging and death designated.
The perfection of generosity was designated.
The perfection of ethical discipline has been proclaimed; the perfection of patience has been proclaimed;
the perfection of vigor has been proclaimed.
The perfection of meditation has been designated,
and the perfection of wisdom has been designated.
But internal emptiness has not been designated.
External emptiness was not designated,
internal-external emptiness was not designated,
and the emptiness of emptiness was not designated.
Great emptiness was not designated, ultimate emptiness was not designated,
and conditioned emptiness was not designated.
Unconditioned emptiness was not designated,
absolute emptiness was not designated,
and the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end was not designated.
Non-dispersal emptiness was not taught;
natural emptiness was not taught; the emptiness of all phenomena was not taught.
Emptiness of specific characteristics was not taught; emptiness of non-apprehension was not taught; emptiness of non-existence was not taught.
Neither the emptiness of intrinsic nature nor the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence has been taught.
Indeed, in this teaching of the Dharma, the applications of mindfulness have not been taught.
The right efforts have not been designated,
the bases of psychic power have not been designated, and the faculties have not been designated.
The powers have not been designated,
the factors of enlightenment have not been designated, and the noble eightfold path has not been designated.
The noble truths are not designated; the meditative absorptions are not designated; the immeasurables are not designated.
The formless attainments have not been designated;
the eight liberations have not been designated; the nine successive meditative attainments have not been designated.
The gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—were not designated;
the superknowledges were not designated; and the meditative concentrations were not designated.
The gateways of dhāraṇī have not been designated;
the powers of a Tathāgata have not been designated; the grounds of self-confidence have not been designated.
The analytical knowledges were not designated, great loving-kindness was not designated,
and great compassion was not designated.
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha have not been designated.
Furthermore, in this teaching of the Dharma, a stream-enterer has not been designated, nor has the fruit of stream-entry been designated;
a once-returner has not been designated, nor has the fruit of once-returning been designated.
The once-returner is not designated, nor is the fruit of once-returning designated;
the arhat is not designated, nor is arhatship designated;
the pratyekabuddha is not designated, nor is pratyekabodhi designated.
Neither a bodhisattva is designated, nor are the bodhisattva stages designated;
neither a Buddha is designated, nor is awakening designated;
nor are syllables designated.
Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to those sons of the gods:
"It is so, sons of the gods; it is so. That awakening of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones is ineffable;
it is beyond verbal expression, and it has not been heard by anyone, nor has it been cognized."
Therefore, O sons of gods, those who wish to abide in the fruit of stream-entry and wish to realize the fruit of stream-entry cannot do so without relying on this patience;
those who wish to abide in the fruit of once-returning and wish to realize the fruit of once-returning cannot do so without relying on this patience;
and those who wish to abide in the fruit of non-returning and wish to realize the fruit of non-returning cannot do so without relying on this patience.
Those who wish to abide in arhatship and wish to realize arhatship do not do so without relying on this patience;
those who wish to abide in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment and wish to realize pratyekabuddha-enlightenment do not do so without relying on this patience;
and those who wish to abide in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment and wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment do not do so without relying on this patience.
Thus indeed, O sons of the gods, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom,
by way of its being beyond verbal expression and hearing.
The fourteenth chapter in the second section of the *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* is completed.
